chapters.n: This short personal letter is about Onesimus, a runaway slave who met Paul and converted. Paul, writing from prison with Timothy, addresses Philemon, a beloved co-worker and slave owner in Colosse.

f.g: Paul is imprisoned because of his service to Christ.

chapters.n: He also greets Apphia (probably Philemon’s wife), Archippus (perhaps their son), and the congregation that meets in Philemon’s home.
The customary greeting of grace and peace from the Father and the Lord Jesus.
Paul always thanks God when he prays for Philemon.
He has heard of Philemon’s faith in the Lord Jesus and his love for all the Saints — the very qualities Paul will now appeal to.
Paul prays that Philemon’s generous sharing of his faith will become effective as he understands every good thing we have in Christ.
Philemon’s love has brought Paul great joy and comfort, because he has refreshed the hearts of the Saints.
So although Paul has the apostolic authority in Christ to order Philemon to do the right thing —
— he would rather appeal to him on the basis of love, as Paul, an old man, and now a prisoner for Christ.
Paul appeals for Onesimus, whom he calls his own son — he became his spiritual father while in chains.

f.g: A common slave name meaning “useful” or “profitable.”
Brought to spiritual birth through conversion.

chapters.n: A playful pun on his name: once he was “useless” to Philemon, but now he is truly “useful” to both of them.
Paul is sending him back — and it feels like sending away his own heart. Receive him.
Paul would have liked to keep Onesimus with him to help him in prison on Philemon’s behalf.

f.g: In your place, on your behalf.

chapters.n: But he won’t do anything without Philemon’s consent, so that any kindness comes freely, not by pressure.
Perhaps Onesimus was separated from Philemon for a little while so that Philemon could have him back forever — Paul sees God’s hand even in his running away.

f.g: For a short time, an hour.

chapters.n: No longer merely as a slave but as more than a slave — a beloved brother. Paul plants a gospel principle that undermines the whole idea of owning a brother.

f.w: in the flesh, and in the Lord
f.g: Both as a person and as a fellow believer.

chapters.n: If you consider me your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.
If he wronged you or owes you anything, charge it to my account. Paul echoes what Christ does for us — taking our debts upon Himself.

f.g: Charge it to me — a bookkeeping term.

chapters.n: Paul writes this pledge in his own handwriting: I will repay it. Then he gently adds that Philemon owes Paul his very soul — Paul likely brought him to Christ.
Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ. Another pun: “benefit” (onaimēn) echoes Onesimus.
Paul writes confident that Philemon will obey — and even do more than Paul asks, perhaps hinting at freeing Onesimus.

f.g: Possibly a hint at granting freedom.

chapters.n: And get a guest room ready for me, because Paul hopes their prayers will lead to his release and a visit. He will see how Onesimus was received!

f.w: I shall be given unto you

chapters.n: Epaphras, Paul’s fellow prisoner and founder of the Colossian branch, sends greetings.
So do Paul’s co-workers Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke — the same group named in Colossians 4.
Paul ends with a blessing: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
